Viscous fingering is a well-known hydrodynamic instability that sets in when a less viscous fluid displaces a more viscous fluid.
The mathematical model used in this study comprises the advection-dispersion equation, Darcy's law, and the divergence-free velocity condition.
The simulation used a viscosity ratio of 33 and a Péclet number of 10,000.
The less viscous fluid tries to move faster than the more viscous fluid due to its higher mobility, leading to the formation of viscous fingers.
The tips of the fingers split and smaller fingers emerge, leading to further stretching of the interface and higher mixing rate across the interface.
Nonlinear mechanisms observed include shielding of one finger by another, merging of fingers, fading of fingers, and channeling of a dominant finger.
Viscous fingering leads to two competing effects: it enhances mixing by increasing interfacial area, but it also causes channeling of the low viscosity fluid, reducing overall mixing efficiency.
The authors developed a two-equation dynamic model for the evolution of concentration variance and mean scalar dissipation rate to quantify the degree of mixing.
The authors used their analysis to predict the range of viscosity contrast that maximizes mixing, though the specific range is not provided.
The computational strategy used in this study is stable for arbitrary viscosity ratios.
Periodic boundary conditions were applied in the transverse direction, and the right edge was a natural flow boundary.
The fluid dynamics video was created from snapshots of the concentration field at successive time steps in the high-resolution numerical simulation.
The displacement is from left to right, with fresh less viscous fluid entering the domain continuously from the left boundary.
Intermediate colors in the simulation denote a mixture of the two pure fluids, with an exponential viscosity-concentration relationship.
The reference frame in the simulation is moving with the average speed of the flow.
